Poilitical groups are allowed to be tax exempt, but not alowed to hide their donations and donors- the money must be transparent. Charitable victim assistance organizations are allowed to hide their donors and who they give money to in order to protect victims. But they are not allowed to engage in political activities. A poorly worded ruling a few years back ("up to 50% of their activities can be political") caused the groups that want to hide where the money came from and where it is going to apply for that particular 501(c) sub category. They are not allowed to be there, and the IRS had to dedicate a lot of resources and take shortcuts to handle the massive jump in applicants. One (of many) things that bother me about the Reddit community is when I'm reading a serious topic and someone derails it with a silly meme comment (broken arms, >9000, etc...). Incredibly to me, more often than not these comments get heavily upvoted and completely derails the original discussion.
How can we, as a community discourage joke/meme comments in serious discussions? Should we?

Shy of clicking the downvoat button (and encouraging others to do the same), I'm not sure there's really much we can do as users. The mods of each 'verse could institute rules for the subs they control and delete joke/meme comments that don't add to the discussion, but that sounds like a moderation nightmare if the site gets bigger.
Had to click that downvoat button when you're still new. I just have been countering it with better (on-topic) comments.

Unfortunately, downvoating a comment won't do much once the size of the community exceeds a certain threshold. Some form of automated moderation (to ensure uniform enforcement) has to be implemented to cut out in-jokes, memes, pun threads, dead-horse phrases, etc. once a sub (or the site) has reached that stage.

As much as I wish voting were the solution, it's simply unrealistic. This conversation is actually where I stray from the opinions of many of the users who have migrated here. Good mods employ good moderation, bad mods employ bad moderation, and you'll notice the teams with their act together are rarely at the heart of meta drama. It's the latter who soil the reputation of those quietly improving a community. I know a lot of great, dedicated mods on the teams I work with and similarly have experience with bad mods. So this raises the question: how do we ensure that the most popular subverses here are staffed with level-headed, fair, clever, and active moderators?

I've been thinking about that, and it's tough. The best idea I've heard is to give the users the ability to vote a mod out of their position. The main problem with reddit is that there is no check on mod power within a sub, so the bad mods can't be stopped. If there is a check of sorts, it could keep mods in line. There would also probably need to be a mandatory investigation whenever a mod gets voted out. Maybe and admin shows up and does some snooping to ensure the mod in question is actually abusing power.

What if every time you submitted a post, you had the option to make it a certain "type" of post? Say for example, you had the option of checking a box labeling the post as a certain type.

If I wanted to post something very morbid and sad, I could make the post a "serious" post. Then, the website would automatically filter comments based on certain things(maybe filter links to popular meme domains, etc.) and perhaps certain users could be temp banned for repeatedly attempting to de-rail serious threads.

If I wanted to make a post on /v/ideasforvoat, I could label the post as "question" or something. Then the community would know by the clear labeling, before even reading the title, that their feedback would be helpful towards the discussion.

If I wanted to post porn here, I could label it as porn/nudity. Then, thumbnails would instantly be censored and bots would instantly scour the net for sauce. This isn't a perfect set of options, but you can see where I am going. Perhaps allow the OP to set the post to multiple groups if they wanted to.

I could see myself scrolling down the front page and seeing small, color coded labels that indicate what the post is attempting to achieve. This would help me sort through /v/all

I see a yellow box next to the title? OP must want users to give him feedback. Perhaps give OP permission to "accept" an answer?

I see a red box next to the title? OP must want to post some quality porn. Perhaps give OP permission to "sticky" the sauce?

I see a blue box next to the title? OP must want to talk about something serious. Perhaps filter comments?

I see a green box next to the title? OP must want to focus on comedy or entertainment or just a generally "open" post.

I see a purple box next to the title? It must be a moderator post or something.

I see an orange box next to the title? I don't know, but you can see how this may help user comprehension.

Now lets say on every page, there are 6 colored boxes on the sidebar, you could click any sequence of those boxes to filter any page you are on to see only certain kinds of posts. Even in a meme subverse, someone may want to have serious discussion about the topic without flocking to an entirely different community.

Voat doesn't want to hamper on free-speech, but you could possibly implement this without giving too much power to bots or OPs.
